summary: Discusses extra considerations for benchmarking network functions that run virtualized on general-purpose hardware. Earlier benchmarking work focused on dedicated physical devices in the lab.

plainLanguage.summary: Testing a toy robot is different from testing a robot that is only software. This lists what to watch for in virtual ones.

questions: black box vs white box benchmarks
subtitle: How to test network functions running in virtualized environments

tldr.problem: Traditional network benchmarking tested dedicated physical devices. Virtual Network Functions run on general-purpose hardware with shared resources, making old testing methods incomplete and results harder to repeat.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC identifies new considerations: document hardware and virtual configurations in detail, test shared-resource scenarios, measure lifecycle stages (activation, operation, deactivation), and track how many virtual instances are needed to match physical device capacity.
tldr.outcome: Benchmarking standards adapted for virtualization help operators compare VNFs fairly and choose the right infrastructure for their needs.

today: RFC 8172 is Informational and remains the IETF's guidance on benchmarking virtual network functions and their infrastructure. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: From Physical to Virtual Network Functions
sections.content:
The Benchmarking Methodology Working Group (BMWG) historically tested physical network devices using standard black-box benchmarks: throughput, latency, and forwarding rates. With Network Function Virtualization (NFV), the same functions now run as software on general-purpose servers, hypervisors, and storage systems.

This change requires new benchmarking approaches. A virtualized environment introduces hardware configuration variables that dedicated devices hide: CPU cores, memory, storage, hypervisor type, and virtual machine settings. Multiple VNFs may share the same hardware. Test repeatability demands documenting all these parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network function moves from a box you buy to software on a computer you share with other software, testing it becomes more complicated.

sections.title: Hardware and Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
VNF benchmarking must document the entire system: the server platform, storage, network interfaces, hypervisor, and virtual machines. The hardware section covers server blades, CPUs, caches, memory, and I/O devices. Configuration parameters include the hypervisor type, number of VMs, virtual network topology, CPU pinning, NUMA node assignment, and the specific VNF functions being tested.

Labs can reuse the same hardware platform for many studies until improvements overtake its capabilities. The separation of hardware and software suppliers means much more internal configuration must now be reported with results to enable comparison testing later.
sections.plainLanguage: Write down what computer, CPU, memory, and software setup you used, so someone else can try the same test and get similar results.

sections.title: Realistic Test Scenarios
sections.content:
Traditional capacity testing at 100% utilization may not represent real deployments. VMs often operate at 50% utilization while sharing processing power. The RFC recommends testing the noisy neighbor problem: one VM in an infinite loop should be isolated so other VMs perform according to specs. Performance variations with long tails and transient errors require longer-term tests.

Elasticity and flexibility are key VNF benefits, so benchmarks must include dynamic scenarios: VMs being created and destroyed, network paths being set up and torn down, and resource allocation changing. Resiliency testing should evaluate recovery approaches enabled by the virtual architecture. The sheer number of test combinations benefits from automation and machine-readable results.
sections.plainLanguage: Test what happens when computers are busy, when one program hogs resources, when you add and remove virtual machines, and when things break and recover.

sections.title: The Shared Resources Challenge
sections.content:
Virtual test components share system resources with the Device Under Test. A virtual machine generating traffic must not share CPU, memory, storage, or network with the VNF being tested, or results will have unexpected dependencies. The RFC advises starting with isolated resources as a baseline, then adding shared-resource scenarios where characteristics of competing load (CPU, memory, storage utilization) are documented and results reconcile with the baseline.

The possibility of using shared resources while producing useful results remains one of the critical challenges to overcome in VNF benchmarking.
sections.plainLanguage: If the tester and the thing being tested fight over the same computer resources, the test results become confusing. Measure with isolated resources first, then measure with sharing and explain what happened.

sections.title: New Benchmarks and Coverage
sections.content:
New benchmark classes address VNF-specific goals: time to deploy VNFs (standing up hundreds of VMs in seconds), time to migrate VNFs to new hardware, and time to create virtual networks. A framework called the 3x3 Matrix organizes benchmarks by life-cycle stage (activation, operation, deactivation) and performance criteria (speed, accuracy, reliability). A 3x4 Matrix adds a scale dimension.

The RFC emphasizes continuing black-box benchmarks—external observations remain essential—while auxiliary white-box metrics (CPU utilization) support operations but do not replace external benchmarks. Traditional packet transfer metrics like one-way delay and packet delay variation should be measured during VNF assessment.
sections.plainLanguage: Measure how fast things turn on and off, how well they work while running, and how big they can grow. Use the same kinds of tests for virtual functions as for physical ones.

sections.title: Power and Resource Consumption
sections.content:
Although benchmarking physical network function power consumption is incomplete, the desire to measure physical infrastructure supporting virtual functions adds to the need. Both maximum power and dynamic power consumption under varying load are valuable. The Intelligent Platform Management Interface (IPMI) standard supports instantaneous energy consumption measurement on many servers.

For virtual resources, energy consumption may be estimated using overall metrics based on utilization readings, though direct measurement remains an open challenge.
sections.plainLanguage: How much electricity does this network function use? Measuring power for virtual functions is harder than measuring it for physical boxes, but the RFC explains what to try.
